title: Hollowtide
description: A fan revival of Asheron's Call, the 1999 MMO I grew up on: a new client for Windows, Mac, Linux, Android (coming soon) and the browser with the community's favorite add-ons built in, on a live server I run. 842 players and 118 releases in its first seven weeks live.

modules.alt: Hollowtide: a player facing an Aetherium Golem on a sunlit coast

modules.html:
Overview

I've wanted to make something like Asheron's Call since I first played it in 1999 on dial-up. AI coding tools are what finally made it possible. Hollowtide is a new game client for the original game, native on Windows, Mac (including Apple Silicon) and Linux, with Android (coming soon), and playable in a browser tab. It connects to a live server I run, with new content on top of the original world.

My role. I'm the designer, director and live-ops lead. I set the vision and the rules, decide what ships, play every build and talk to players. The code is written by AI coding agents (Claude Code) working from my direction, design docs and decisions, several at once. In the twelve weeks since the first commit that was 8,620 commits and nearly 900 design, plan and findings documents. Every release went out on my explicit go.

It's like running a small studio where every engineer is an agent. My job was the same as on a game team: find the real player problem, decide what good looks like, make it testable, and hold the line on quality.

What Hollowtide stands for

I played on Darktide, and I watched Asheron's Call go years without real updates toward the end of retail. Hollowtide is my answer as a player and as a UX designer for games: making the game what I always wanted it to be, on four principles.

  • Fix what bugged players about retail. Take out the friction, not the challenge: the Assistant built in, inventory search that finds item sets, a pack Sort button, junk sold in one press at a vendor, saved logins, several characters in one app, controller support, a password reset on the login screen, and hundreds more.
  • Balance first. No wild changes to the core loops, the classes or the economy. My test for anything players can earn: if it makes the hardest end-game places easy, it's too strong.
  • Approachable for new and old players. Nothing to install, and a newcomer can find their way without a wiki open in another window.
  • A PK-driven revival of Darktide. Open player killing from level 10, PK Night every other Sunday, and tools that help players find and join an allegiance.

modules.html:
The problem: the hardest part of playing was getting in

Asheron's Call shut down in 2017. Fans kept it alive on community servers, but playing today means:

  • An original 32-bit Windows client that needs workarounds on a modern PC and doesn't run natively on a Mac.
  • Third-party add-ons that veterans call mandatory (VTank for combat and looting, maps, radars), each installed separately through a separate plugin framework.
  • The original game's data files, which a new player has to find on their own.

On our first public launch night, October 9, nobody from outside the project even reached the login screen. The download wasn't the barrier. The setup was. Three design goals came out of that:

  1. Feel like the original. Veterans notice small differences in movement and casting right away. If it doesn't feel like the game they remember, nothing else matters.
  2. Build the add-ons in. Everything players used to install is part of the client, on by default where it helps, and compatible with their old files.
  3. One click to play. A browser link should put a new player in the world in about a minute.

One click to play, in the browser

After launch night I made the call to build a browser version. It was live two days later: a player opens a link, picks a name and is in Holtburg about a minute later, with nothing to install. A guest can keep their character later by choosing a password, and an Invite a friend button copies a link that tells the friend who invited them.

Designing for the browser meant real constraints: low-end laptops (the game lowers its own render resolution when the graphics card struggles), browser shortcuts that fight game keys (F5, Alt+Left, Tab), and slow connections (your own armor downloads first, so you never arrive undressed).

modules.name: browser
modules.label: From the browser page to walking in Holtburg in under 30 seconds, with nothing installed

modules.html:
It worked. In the first three weeks, 396 of the 419 players who entered the world played in the browser. Seven weeks in, it's still 771 of 842.

The same thinking is taking the game to phones. The Android app (coming soon) puts the browser version's touch controls (a stick, buttons and a menu wheel) into the game itself, and a phone that opens the web page is offered the app before the download starts.

modules.alt: Players per day, October 3 to 23: almost none before the browser version, then a peak of 164 on October 16 and a steady 25 to 40 a day after

modules.html:
"Feel like the original," made testable

You can't fix "it feels off." So I made the original client the judge. The 1999 client runs on a test machine, and a harness drives it and our client through the same inputs and compares positions, timing, animation and what the server is told. Movement passes 69 of 69 of those cases on every release, and the network layer is checked against replays of recorded sessions of the original client.

Where I chose to differ from the original on purpose, it's written down with a reason and approved before it ships: for example, a 10-second rescue when a spell cast gets stuck, while keeping the original's rule that you hold still to cast. Matching the original is the default; every exception is a design decision.

A player's report shows how this pays off. One veteran told us that holding strafe and turn, then pressing run, moved differently from the original. We recorded both clients doing it, found the rule, added it to the tests and shipped the fix the next day, with a thank-you in the patch notes.

The add-ons, built in

  • The Assistant (VTank built in): auto attack, healing, buffing, looting, salvage, mana and navigation routes drawn in the world. Players' old route and loot files load as they are.
  • A searchable world map you can zoom from one town to the whole continent, with your own pins and a go arrow.
  • Item comparison, an in-game wiki (F1) and a radar with walls and coordinates.
  • A Leveling Guide in the in-game wiki built from the server's own data, where every place name is a link that points the go arrow at it.

The design work was mostly about trust. An automation that acts for you has to explain itself: hovering the Assistant shows what it's doing and its last five actions, a red ring says when something you turned on can't work and why, and it leaves your hands alone for 30 seconds after you wield something yourself.

modules.html:
Guidance: from "where do I go?" to a Journal that knows

Asheron's Call never told you where to go. That's part of its charm for veterans and a wall for everyone else, and the funnel showed it: 54% of the players who arrived in the first three weeks never passed level 1. I designed guidance in layers, lightest first, so veterans can ignore it:

  • Tips at the moment they matter, once each: your first death, first resist, first time over-burdened. One Hide tips turns them all off.
  • A gold arrow to your first hunt after a minute in town, and quest givers that mark themselves only when you meet their level.
  • Long NPC speeches end with one short gold line saying what they want, with Track and Go.
  • The Journal became the home for quests: Active, Waiting, Done and Available, a Next step for each, "Where next" for hunting grounds at your level, and directions that use portals and your recalls.
  • A quest tracker on screen that leads you into buildings and up stairs.

items.name: journal
items.alt: The Journal's Next step, with a first-hour tip above it

items.name: tracker
items.alt: The on-screen quest tracker pointing toward a turn-in (opt-in while it's tested)

modules.html:
The tracker taught me the most. Its first version pointed players at places where nothing was, so I pulled it from players' screens and kept it opt-in while we audited every hint against the world itself. In the audit, 351 of 2,579 "where to get it" sources couldn't actually give the item, 252 hints pointed at NPCs this server never spawns, and 27 travel routes were impossible. All three went to zero. The Journal shipped to everyone; the on-screen tracker waits until it's right.

Among players who arrived after the first three weeks, 43% never passed level 1. That's better, but the newcomers changed too (fewer veterans, more passers-by), so I don't claim the guidance did it alone.

modules.alt: From first visit to regular: 348 entered the world, 44% reached level 2, 36% reached level 5, 16% played on two or more days

modules.html:
A world that feels alive with a small population

Early on there were only a handful of players online, and an empty MMO feels dead. Three design answers:

  • New content on the server: world bosses on a timer with telegraphed attacks and personal loot (the Forge-Warden of Ispar, Old Snapjaw, Varrow the Unbowed), new creatures and regions, new weapons and a nine-piece armor set, pets, and a festival calendar that runs every year.
  • The Hollow Company: mercenaries who roam Holtburg, talk in General chat and join your fellowship if you invite them. They're clearly labeled as not players and never counted in the online number. A busy town, never a fake population.
  • Founders: everyone who made an account before November gets a shirt, a house banner and a title, for life.

modules.html:
Bringing back the events the original retired

Asheron's Call ran monthly story events for 17 years, and almost all of them were switched off for good when their month ended. Veterans remember them, and a date on the calendar is the best reason I have found for a lapsed player to log in tonight. So I had every one of them catalogued, 75 events from 1999 to 2017, and put them on a calendar that repeats every year, rebuilt from the original as closely as the records allow, with their rewards back.

The first are running now: Fowl Play (November 20 to 30) and Bael'Zharon's Rampage (November 24 to 30), where the original game's great villain visits 16 towns. Each one is played through by bots on a test server and by me before it goes live.

Player killing, and letting the data pick the fix

Hollowtide runs Darktide rules: anyone can attack anyone, anywhere, the way the original's PK server did. It's the identity of the server, and it creates the obvious design worry: new players get killed by veterans and quit.

Instead of guessing, I looked. Kills of characters under level 20 were running 15 to 67 a week, so I extended the newcomer protection to level 10, my one exception to the original rules. The next week it was 5. And of the players under level 30 whose first death to another player came in November, 23 of 38 (61%) came back on a later day. Ganking hurt, but it wasn't the main reason people left. Getting people in the door was.

A study of the other PK servers showed what keeps their players: something to fight for, and something to fight in, at any hour. So the PK work now goes there:

  • PK Night: every Sunday at a set time and place, with a reward for the allegiance that holds the ground.
  • Newcomer protection to level 10, and a short note after your first death to another player: where your corpse is, how long it stays, where to get buffed again, who is recruiting, and the next PK Night (in progress).
  • Darktide Season 1, opening December 6: a fresh ladder, and trophies only for honourable kills (no credit for farming newcomers or alts), spent at PK vendors (built, going live with the season).
  • An arena queue for 1v1, 2v2 and free-for-all fights on demand, with no item loss (in progress).

Quality of life, in the hundreds

Most of the work players actually feel is small. A few favorites:

  • A login screen that tells the truth: Online, Restarting or Maintenance, players on, your ping, and a countdown to the nightly restart. "Is it me or the server?" is the first question when something goes wrong.
  • Drag shows where an item will land: a green ring, or a red sign where it can't go.
  • Drop gear on another player to hand it over. Giving is far more common than trading.
  • Chat tabs that sort themselves, so spell words and system lines stop drowning out conversation.
  • The disconnect screen says why: a planned update, the nightly restart, or your connection.
  • Your windows and settings follow your character to another computer, including the browser.
  • Map pins you place yourself, and dungeon names on the map.
  • Looking for Group: post what you need, then join a fellowship right from the Fellowship panel.
  • The Escape menu tells you if your client is up to date.

Running it live

I treated the launch as a series of small beats, each a new reason to invite people and each small enough for the server and me to handle:

  • October 3, soft launch: a small group of players finds the rough edges.
  • October 9, first public post to the Asheron's Call community. Nobody got past setup, which led straight to the browser version.
  • October 11, the browser version goes live, with Founders and Invite a friend. October 13, the Discord opens.
  • October 15 and 16, the browser post and a Holtburg meet-up at a set time, with the game moved to hollowtide.org. More than 200 new players entered the world in those two days.
  • In the week of November 14 to 20, 102 different players logged in, 26 to 42 a day, and 34 of them played on three or more of those days.

I kept it deliberately low-key: community channels only, free to play, no press. The right first audience is the people who love the original, and the pitch is the easiest way to play, never a reason to leave another server.

The community around us matters as much as our own. Our players chat with players on other servers through the Dereth Network's shared Global channel. Hollowtide is listed in ThwargLauncher and WebAC, so veterans can play it on the original client with Decal and their plugins, and a player who arrives that way gets one line pointing at our client.

The feedback loop

  • F7 files a bug report from inside the game, with a snapshot and where you were standing. Players have sent 438 written reports from 58 different people, and the client's own watchdog has sent 869 automatic ones.
  • A new-bug alarm compares each release with the last one per hour of real play, so a regression shows up within hours.
  • Fixes come back with credit: each release post thanks the players whose reports drove it.
  • A Feature Requests board in the game: players suggest and vote, and see what's planned, done or declined, and why.

modules.name: requests
modules.alt: The in-game Feature Requests board: player ideas with votes and a status for each

modules.html:
Learning to slow down

The first weeks shipped fast: 71 releases in 21 days, 9 of them on October 16 alone. Speed got fixes to players within hours, but in that stretch one fix broke teleports and had to be pulled, and players on old versions kept reporting bugs that were already fixed. So I set a stability plan:

  1. Every fixed bug gets a replay test that runs before each release.
  2. One planned release a day, after a soak: bots play the candidate for about 20 minutes, and it ships only if its error rate is no worse than the live version's.
  3. Old clients are asked to update: a browser tab offers a reload, and the desktop app asks at login.
  4. Reports are grouped in a daily digest, so a genuinely new bug stands out.

Since then it has held at one or two releases a day: 46 more from October 24 to November 21, each soaked first.

Results

12 weeksfrom first commit (August 28) to today; seven weeks live
842players entered the world (October 3 to November 21)
92%of them played in the browser, with nothing to install
About 7,100hours played by real players
195players came back on two or more days; 56 have played more than 10 hours, and 24 more than 100
1,307player reports, written and automatic, read and triaged
118releases, the first 71 in 21 days, then a soaked release a day
69 of 69movement tests match the original 1999 client

What I learned

  • The barrier is rarely the one you plan for. I built a native client for three platforms, and launch night showed the real wall was setup. The browser version now carries 92% of players.
  • The barrier moves. Seven weeks in, the wall isn't setup or level 1 any more: it's that new people stop hearing about the game. New players per week fell from over 300 to under 100 while the regulars held steady, so the work moved from the first hour to giving people a dated reason to come, every week.
  • Check the scary assumption. Everyone, me included, assumed ganking drove new players away. 61% of first-time victims came back, so I fixed the worst of it and spent the rest of the effort on reasons to fight.
  • Make "feel" measurable. Using the original client as the judge turned arguments about feel into tests that pass or fail, and let me approve each intentional difference on purpose.
  • Shipping fast is a tool, not a virtue. Same-day fixes built trust with players. The day one of them broke teleports, a soak and a replay test per fix were cheaper than another apology.
  • Guidance has to be true before it's helpful. A quest arrow that points nowhere is worse than no arrow.
  • Directing AI agents is directing a team. The leverage is real, but it's still design: clear goals, written decisions, a definition of done that can be checked, and someone who plays every build.

What's next

  • Get more people in: a dated reason to play every week (PK Night, the yearly events, Season 1), posted where veterans are, and a measure of what each post brings in.
  • Darktide Season 1 on December 6, and the arena queue, so there's a fight worth having at any hour.
  • A town decorator: an in-game tool for laying out a town's props, starting with Holtburg. It's staff-only for now, a first step toward players proposing content and me approving it. (I shelved the bigger dungeon builder to do this.)
  • Turn the on-screen quest tracker on for everyone once its hints pass the accuracy audit.

The server also runs the Borg, a faction of bots that level, hunt and fight on the live server. How I'm teaching them to experiment instead of following my rulebook is its own case study: Teaching Bots to Experiment.

Numbers are from the live server's event log, October 3 to November 21, 2026, counting real players only (no staff, no bots, no mercenaries). A player is one account; a browser guest who clears their browser and comes back counts again.
